description: Composite figure (Fig. 9); two of the three panels were supplied. (b) is a grouped bar chart: y-axis "Austenitic volume fraction/%" from 0 to 100 with gridlines every 20; x-axis shows the four steel conditions QA-620, QA-680, QA-740, QA-800; the legend distinguishes red "Before tensile" bars from blue "After tensile" bars. (c) is a dual-axis dot-line chart with x-axis "Steels" (same four conditions), left axis "k" (0.0–2.0, tick step 0.5) and right axis "SFE/mJ m⁻²" (30–40, tick step 2); black circles joined by a line give k and red squares joined by a line give SFE, with printed data labels k = 1.24, 0.56, 1.47, 1.50 and SFE = 36.50, 38.27, 33.29, 31.53 mJ m⁻² for QA-620, QA-680, QA-740, QA-800 respectively. Panel (a), XRD profiles before and after tensile testing, is described by the caption but absent from the supplied image set. Together the panels argue that the annealed austenite partially transforms to martensite during tension (TRIP) in all four conditions, and that the k value varies inversely with SFE, the minimum k (QA-680) coinciding with the maximum SFE and thus the highest austenitic stability.

Dual-axis dot-line chart, x-axis 'Steels' (QA-620, QA-680, QA-740, QA-800), left axis k (0.0-2.0), right axis SFE/mJ m⁻² (30-40). Black circles (k) and red squares (SFE) with printed labels: k = 1.24, 0.56, 1.47, 1.50 and SFE = 36.50, 38.27, 33.29, 31.53. The two quantities move in opposite directions, crossing between QA-680 and QA-740.

observations.observation: Panel (b) is a grouped bar chart whose legend has two entries printed exactly as 'Before tensile' (red) and 'After tensile' (blue).
Panel (b) y-axis is labelled 'Austenitic volume fraction/%' and runs from 0 to 100 in steps of 20; the four x categories are QA-620, QA-680, QA-740 and QA-800.
In panel (b) the before-tensile (red) bar is taller than the after-tensile (blue) bar for all four conditions, showing that the austenitic volume fraction decreased during the tensile test.
In panel (b) the QA-740 before-tensile bar is the tallest, its top lying just above the 50% gridline, while the QA-620 after-tensile bar is the shortest of all eight bars.
No numeric value labels are printed on the bars of panel (b); only gridlines allow relative comparison of bar heights.
Panel (c) has two y-axes: left 'k' (0.0 to 2.0, step 0.5) and right 'SFE/mJ m⁻²' (30 to 40, step 2), with x-axis labelled 'Steels' listing QA-620, QA-680, QA-740 and QA-800.
Printed k data labels in panel (c) are 1.24 (QA-620), 0.56 (QA-680), 1.47 (QA-740) and 1.50 (QA-800), so k is minimum at QA-680 and maximum at QA-800.
Printed SFE data labels in panel (c) are 36.50, 38.27, 33.29 and 31.53 for QA-620, QA-680, QA-740 and QA-800 respectively, i.e. maximum at QA-680 and decreasing monotonically above 680 °C.
The k curve and the SFE curve in panel (c) show opposite trends: the minimum of k (QA-680) coincides with the maximum of SFE, and the two lines cross between QA-680 and QA-740.

The caption states that panel (a) shows XRD profiles of QA specimens before and after tensile test, panel (b) an austenitic volume fraction bar chart, and panel (c) dot-line charts of k, the austenitic stability constant, and SFE.
The citing text states the estimated SFEs of the QA specimens lie between 20 mJ/m² and 40 mJ/m², implying TWIP as well as TRIP behaviour during deformation.
The citing text states that QA-740 and QA-800 have the two highest k values (~1.47 and ~1.50) and that QA-680 has the lowest (~0.56), showing little austenite-to-martensite transformation.
The citing text asserts that a higher k value corresponds to lower austenitic mechanical stability, so the k variation with annealing temperature is opposite to the SFE variation.
The citing text concludes that TRIP, in addition to TWIP, occurred in all specimens because the austenitic fraction after tensile testing was lower than that before testing despite SFE > 20 mJ/m².
